segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So what I’m going to talk about to you today is something called Ethnography.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This is a type of research aimed at exploring the way human cultures work.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It was first developed for use in anthropology, and it’s also been used in sociology and communication studies.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So what’s it got to do with business, you may ask.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Well, businesses are finding that ethnography can offer them deeper insight into the possible needs of customers, either present or future, as well as providing valuable information about their attitudes towards existing products.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And ethnography can also help companies to design new products or services that customers really want.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Let’s look at some examples of how ethnographic research works in business.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: One team of researchers did a project for a company manufacturing kitchen equipment.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: They watched how cooks used measuring cups to measure out things like sugar and flour.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: They saw that the cooks had to check and recheck the contents, because although the measuring cups had numbers inside them, the cooks couldn’t see these easily.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So a new design of cup was developed to overcome this problem, and it was a top seller.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Another team of ethnographic researchers looked at how cell phones were used in Uganda, in Africa.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: They found that people who didn’t have their own phones could pay to use the phones of local entrepreneurs.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Because these customers paid in advance for their calls, they were eager to know how much time they’d spent on the call so far.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So the phone company designed phones for use globally with this added feature.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Ethnographic research has also been carried out in computer companies.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In one company, IT systems administrators were observed for several weeks.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It was found that a large amount of their work involved communicating with colleagues in order to solve problems, but that they didn’t have a standard way of exchanging information from spreadsheets and so on.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So the team came up with an idea for software that would help them to do this. In another piece of research, a team observed and talked to nurses working in hospitals.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This led to the recognition that the nurses needed to access the computer records of their patients, no matter where they were.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This led to the development of a portable computer tablet that allowed the nurses to check records in locations throughout the hospital.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Occasionally, research can be done even in environments where the researchers can’t be present.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For example, in one project done for an airline, respondents used their smartphones to record information during airline trips, in a study aiming at tracking the emotions of passengers during a flight. ——————— So what makes studies like these different from ordinary research?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Let’s look at some of the general principles behind ethnographic research in business.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: First of all, the researcher has to be completely open-minded – he or she hasn’t thought up a hypothesis to be tested, as is the case in other types of research.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Instead they wait for the participants in the research to inform them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: As far as choosing the participants themselves is concerned, that’s not really all that different from ordinary research – the criteria according to which the participants are chosen may be something as simple as the age bracket they fall into, or the researchers may select them according to their income, or they might try to find a set of people who all use a particular product, for example.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But it’s absolutely crucial to recruit the right people as participants.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: As well as the criteria I’ve mentioned, they have to be comfortable talking about themselves and being watched as they go about their activities.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Actually, most researchers say that people open up pretty easily, maybe because they’re often in their own home of workplace.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So what makes this type of research special is that it’s not just a matter of sending a questionnaire to the participants, instead the research is usually based on first-hand observation of what they are doing at the time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But that doesn’t mean that the researcher never talks to the participants.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: However, unlike in traditional research, in this case it’s the participant rather than the researchers who decides what direction the interview will follow.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This means that there’s less likelihood of the researcher imposing his or her own ideas on the participant.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But after they’ve said goodbye to their participants and got back to their office, the researchers’ work isn’t finished.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Most researchers estimate that 70 to 80 per cent of their time is spent not on the collecting of data but on its analysis – looking at photos listening to recording and transcribing them and so on.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The researchers may end up with hundreds of pages of notes.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And to determine what’s significant, they don’t focus on the sensational things or the unusual things, instead they try to identify a pattern of some sort in all this data, and to discern the meaning behind it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This can result in some compelling insights that can in turn feed back to the whole design process.
